{{Short description|Compound shape made of identical uniform polyhedra arranged uniformly}}

In [[geometry]], a '''uniform polyhedron compound''' is a [[polyhedral compound]] whose constituents are identical (although possibly [[chirality|enantiomorphous]]) [[uniform polyhedron|uniform polyhedra]], in an arrangement that is also uniform, i.e. the [[symmetry group]] of the compound acts [[Orbit (group theory)|transitively]] on the compound's [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]].

The uniform polyhedron compounds were first enumerated by John Skilling in 1976, with a proof that the enumeration is complete. The following table lists them according to his numbering.

The prismatic compounds of {{nowrap|{{math|{''p''/''q''}-}}gonal}} [[Prism (geometry)|prism]]s ([[prismatic compound of prisms with rotational freedom|UC<sub>20</sub>]] and [[prismatic compound of prisms|UC<sub>21</sub>]]) exist only when {{math|{{sfrac|''p''|''q''}} > 2}}, and when {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}} are [[Coprime integers|coprime]]. The uniform prismatic compounds of {{nowrap|{{math|{''p''/''q''}-}}gonal}} [[antiprism]]s ([[Prismatic compound of antiprisms with rotational freedom|UC<sub>22</sub>]], [[Prismatic compound of antiprisms|UC<sub>23</sub>]], [[Prismatic compound of antiprisms with rotational freedom|UC<sub>24</sub>]] and [[Prismatic compound of antiprisms|UC<sub>25</sub>]]) exist only when {{math|{{sfrac|''p''|''q''}} > {{sfrac|3|2}}}}, and when {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}} are coprime. Furthermore, when {{math|1={{sfrac|''p''|''q''}} = 2}}, the antiprisms [[Degeneracy (mathematics)|degenerate]] into [[tetrahedra]] with [[digon]]al bases.
